第1-2题: Students at Greenhill University will notice several changes in the dining hall this term. From next Monday, the two main cafeterias will stop handing out plastic forks, knives and spoons with takeaway meals. Diners who want cutlery will pick up a reusable set at the counter and pay a deposit of two dollars, which is returned when the set comes back. Paper straws replaced the plastic ones last month, and cold drinks are now sold in cans or glass bottles instead of plastic cups. The head of campus services, Dana Whitfield, said the trial follows a survey in which nearly seventy percent of students said they would support such a move. She admitted that the deposit system might slow the lunch queue in the first few weeks, and said extra staff would be on hand to help. If the trial goes well, the university plans to extend it to the coffee shops in the library and the sports centre.
第3-4题: A non-profit group in the town of Westbrook is opening a free summer coding camp for teenagers aged thirteen to seventeen. The camp will run for four weeks in July, with classes on weekday mornings from nine until twelve. Students will learn the basics of building a simple website, and by the end of the course each of them will have designed a small page about a subject they care about. Organisers say there is room for sixty students and that no previous experience is required. Applications opened on Monday and will close at the end of May. Those who cannot easily travel to the town centre can take a bus that leaves from three neighbourhood schools each morning. The group's director, Peter Nash, said the camp began three years ago with twelve teenagers and a single classroom. Last summer, he added, more than half of the students who finished the course went on to take a computer science class at school.
第5-7题: Lakeside Park will stay open until eleven at night from this Friday, three hours later than usual, as part of a two-month trial. The city council says the aim is to give residents somewhere to walk and exercise after work, especially in the hot summer months when daytime temperatures keep many people indoors. New lights have been fitted along the main path around the lake, and two more security guards will patrol the park in the evenings. The boating area and the children's playground, however, will still close at eight, because staff are needed to check the equipment every night. Not everyone is pleased. A group of residents living near the east gate has written to the council, arguing that late-night noise and parking problems are likely to get worse. The council has promised to review the complaints after the first month and to shorten the opening hours if the disturbance becomes serious. A final decision on whether to keep the later closing time will be made in September.
第8-11题: W: Greenhill Sports Centre, Sophie speaking. How can I help? M: Hi, um, I am a second-year student and I was thinking of joining the gym. I mean, I have never really used one before, so I am not sure where to start. W: No problem. We have two kinds of membership. The full one is ninety dollars a term and gives you everything, the weights room, the pool and all the classes. The basic one is fifty, but it covers only the weights room and the pool.

M: Right. And, sorry, does the basic one include the pool at weekends? Someone told me it is closed on Sundays. W: The pool is open every day, but on Sunday it closes at four instead of nine. M: OK, that is fine. I think I would go for the full one, because I would like to try a class. What sort of classes are there? W: Well, there is yoga on Monday and Wednesday mornings, spinning, that is the exercise bikes, on Tuesday and Thursday evenings, and a beginners' fitness class on Saturday at ten.

M: Saturday at ten might work. Is it very hard? I am, er, not exactly fit at the moment. W: It is designed for people who have not exercised for a while. The instructor keeps the group small, twelve people at most, so she can check everyone's technique. M: Sounds good. Do I need to book, or can I just turn up? W: You need to book, and places go quickly. Booking opens a week before each class, online or at the desk.

M: Got it. And one more thing, can I pay by card, or is it cash only? W: Card is fine. If you sign up before Friday there is a ten percent discount for new members. M: Oh, nice. I will come in tomorrow then. W: Great. Ask for me at the desk.
第12-15题: W: So, have you looked at the train times for the trip? M: I have, and honestly it is more expensive than I expected. A return ticket to the coast is eighty dollars each. W: Eighty? That is, wow. Last year it was about fifty. M: I know. But there is a slower train that takes five hours instead of three, and that one is only forty-five.

W: Five hours is a lot. Though I suppose we could leave early and sleep on the train. What about somewhere to stay? M: That is the other thing. The hotels near the beach are all over a hundred a night. But I found a hostel about twenty minutes' walk from the water, beds from thirty dollars, and breakfast is included. W: A hostel. Hmm. Is it, you know, shared rooms? M: Four to a room. I have stayed in worse. And the reviews say it is clean, which matters more to me than privacy for two nights.

W: Fair enough. So if we take the slow train and the hostel, that is, what, about a hundred and fifty each for travel and beds? M: Closer to a hundred and sixty with the bus from the station. But we would still need food, and, um, the boat trip you wanted. W: The boat trip is sixty. I would rather skip one dinner out and do that, actually. M: Agreed. But let us not book the boat until we see the weather. If it rains, that money is gone.

W: Good point. Shall I book the hostel tonight, then? The cheap beds might go. M: Yes, do it. I will sort out the train tomorrow when I get paid. W: And I will check the forecast on Thursday. M: Perfect. Bring the details to lunch and we can work out the rest.
第16-18题: Most students take notes in class, but few are ever taught how to do it well. The result is often a page of sentences copied word for word from a slide, which feels productive at the time and turns out to be almost useless a month later.

Research on memory suggests three simple habits that make a real difference. The first is to write in your own words. When you rephrase an idea, your brain has to process it, and that effort is what fixes it in memory. Copying, by contrast, lets the words pass from the screen to the page without ever being understood.

The second habit is to leave space. A page packed with text gives you nowhere to add a question, an example or a correction when you review the material. Many students find that a wide margin down one side of the page is enough, and they use it later to sum up each paragraph in a single line.

The third habit is to review your notes within a day. Reading them once, twenty-four hours after the lecture, does more than reading them five times the week before an exam. The reason is that forgetting has already begun, and pulling the information back takes a little effort, the same effort that strengthens the memory. None of these habits takes extra time in class. They simply change what you do with the pen in your hand.
第19-21题: I spent last autumn volunteering at a community kitchen in my neighbourhood, and it changed the way I think about free time. I had signed up mostly out of guilt. A friend had been going for a year and kept saying how much she enjoyed it, and I had run out of excuses.

The first Saturday I arrived at seven in the morning, was handed an apron and a box of onions, and spent two hours cutting them. Nobody thanked me. Nobody even asked my name. I went home smelling of onions and wondering whether I would go back.

I did go back, mainly because the woman in charge, Nora, remembered me the following week and put me on the serving counter. That was different. Standing there with a ladle in my hand, I met the same faces every Saturday: a retired teacher who came for the soup and stayed for the conversation, two brothers who always arrived late, and a young father who never asked for anything for himself.

What I learned was not the lesson I expected. I had thought volunteering was about giving something up. In practice, it gave a shape to my week. Saturday morning stopped being a space I had to fill and became the part I looked forward to. I am not suggesting that everyone should spend their weekends in a kitchen. But I would say this: the first visit is the hardest, and it is worth getting through.
第22-25题: Buying clothes online has one obvious disadvantage: you cannot try them on. Shops know this, which is why most of them now offer free returns within a set number of days. The rules, however, differ far more than most customers realise.

The first thing to check is the deadline. Thirty days from delivery is common, but some sellers count from the day you place the order, which can take a week off your time. Second, look at what counts as 'unused'. A pair of shoes worn indoors once is usually fine; shoes with mud on the soles are not. Tags must normally still be attached, and many sellers refuse anything that smells of perfume or smoke. Most also expect the item to return in its original packaging.

Third, decide how to send the item back. A prepaid label is convenient, but the cost is sometimes deducted from your refund, so a cheaper postal service may be worth the extra walk. Keep the receipt until the money arrives. Finally, photograph the parcel before you hand it over, especially if it contains more than one item. Parcels do go missing, and a picture of the sealed box, with the label clearly visible, settles most arguments quickly. None of this takes long. Five minutes of checking before you click 'buy' will save you a month of emails later.
